item.title: Explosions heard in Saudi capital Riyadh
item.description:
Multiple explosions were heard in the Saudi capital on Tuesday, as the military coalition fighting Yemen’s Houthis said it had intercepted a ballistic missile launched by the Iran-backed group towards Riyadh.
AFP journalists heard the blasts and residents received an alert on their mobile phones instructing them to take shelter due to an “aerial threat.”
“Air defenses intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia towards Riyadh,” the Saudi-led coalition posted on X.
A subsequent message from the country’s civil defense agency said the danger had passed.
The coalition had earlier said air defenses also destroyed a ballistic missile headed towards the southern region overnight.
Saudi Arabia, the world’s biggest oil exporter, has faced near-daily strikes from the Houthis for weeks, after a truce in their long-running conflict unraveled in July.
On Sunday, the Houthis claimed attacks on Riyadh’s business district, where witnesses said the Aramco Tower was damaged.
Saudi authorities said the building suffered minor damage from falling shrapnel after an “attempted attack.”
Images released by Saudi Arabia’s press agency on Tuesday showed the Riyadh region’s deputy governor and other officials inspecting the building, with visible damage to some of its floors.
The Houthis have repeatedly targeted Aramco tankers, refineries, storage areas and the company’s headquarters.
The coalition has in response been launching airstrikes against Houthi positions inside Yemen.
According to Houthi news agency Saba, Saudi warplanes on Tuesday carried out a series of strikes on the capital Sanaa and its outskirts, targeting a gas facility and a building belonging to the Yemeni state oil company.
The coalition initially began fighting the Houthis in March 2015, months after the group seized Sanaa and forced out Yemen’s internationally recognized government.

item.title: French students block dozens of schools
item.description:
French students blocked the entrances to dozens of high schools on Tuesday, the education ministry said, as they kept up protests for better learning conditions.
Student protests across France since September have spiraled into larger cost-of-living demonstrations in recent weeks, some marked by fringe violence and accusations of police brutality.
The unrest comes ahead of elections to replace President Emmanuel Macron next year.
With the European Union’s second-largest economy under pressure to rein in debt, the government has limited scope to appease protesters through additional spending.
Forty-nine of the country’s 3,700 high schools for 15 to 18-year-olds were blockaded on Tuesday morning, the ministry said. Authorities expected several thousand school and university students at a Paris protest on Tuesday afternoon.
“Now is the time to step up the mobilization by continuing to put pressure on the government,” student and teacher unions said in a joint statement released Monday.
Student association leader Ryad Rani said it was essential to keep up the pressure.
“We’re not just fighting for ourselves. We’re fighting for teachers, for their working conditions,” he said.
The government has announced measures including the gradual replacement of an online selection platform to access higher education, as well as financial means for some of the worst-off schools.
But students say this is not enough.
Unions are not happy either, with one leader saying on Monday that a government pledge to increase to the minimum wage by 0.6% on top of a standard adjustment for inflation was “crumbs.”
They have called for a new day of strikes and protest on November 17.
Around 575,000 people demonstrated across the country during cost-of-living strikes and protests last Thursday, according to authorities. Unions put the number at 1.5 million.

item.title: Trump sees 'positive momentum' on Iran after Qatar PM talks
item.description:
US President Donald Trump said on Monday there was momentum toward ending the war with Iran, as he declared that the country "militarily is effectively over," but kept open the possibility of new strikes.
Trump met at the White House with Qatar Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani -- a key mediator in the Iran war. It was his first meeting with a foreign leader since his party's massive losses in the midterm elections.
Trump later posted on Truth Social that the two leaders had "an excellent conversation" and that "much was discussed with respect to the Islamic Republic of Iran."
In the weeks leading up to the midterms, there was widespread speculation that US strikes against Iran would resume soon after.
However, Trump has talked down resuming the conflict while leaving the door open to further strikes -- a position he reiterated Monday at a White House press briefing.
"Iran, militarily, is effectively over. We're just keeping it the status quo," Trump told reporters. "But if we do have to go back in, we are locked and loaded, and ready to go."
In his social post on Monday, Trump said that he believed further strikes were "quite unlikely" given that key US allies in the Gulf "would prefer the status quo."
"We are seeing positive momentum toward an end to this Conflict, and will ensure that America's interests are at all times protected," Trump said.
Iranian officials meanwhile expressed defiance at the continued pressure from Washington.
The Islamic republic's top security chief, Mohsen Rezai, wrote on X late Monday that the US "flails like a desperate gambler," telling Washington to "fold your hand. Stop manufacturing fake news about imaginary talks."
Earlier, Tehran's top negotiator Mahammad Bagher Ghalibaf claimed on X that Israel was pushing the US deeper into conflict, adding that "unless Washington drops the 'Israel First' mindset, America and its allies are headed straight for a dark age."
On the ground in Iran, strikes -- which have not been publicly acknowledged by the US military -- are continuing, according to Iranian authorities.
The island of Qeshm, located in the Strait of Hormuz, was targeted overnight from Sunday to Monday, the provincial deputy governor stated on state television.
Trump has acknowledged that the highly unpopular war with Iran was at least partially responsible for the Republicans' defeat, not least because it has contributed to rising prices in the US economy.

item.title: Ishraque: Hasina’s return in December claims political propaganda
item.description:
Former state minister and Dhaka-6 MP Ishraque Hossain has said the process of bringing former prime minister Sheikh Hasina back to Bangladesh through an extradition treaty and an Interpol Red Notice has already begun.
"We seek her return under an extradition treaty. At the same time, the process of bringing her back through an Interpol Red Notice has also been initiated. We want a convicted perpetrator of genocide and murder brought back to face justice in Bangladesh. Anything else you are hearing is nothing more than political manoeuvring or propaganda," he said.
He made the remarks while responding to questions from journalists after a meeting on the law-and-order situation in Dhaka district on Tuesday morning.
Ishraque said Bangladesh, with a population of around 180 million, has only about 200,000 police personnel, excluding members of the Ansar and Village Defence Party (VDP). As a result, law enforcement agencies alone cannot maintain control over every aspect of the situation, making political initiatives necessary alongside their efforts.
"We held parliamentary and party meetings yesterday, where the prime minister issued strict directives. Each of us, as MPs, will organise political resistance in our respective constituencies, working alongside party activists and the general public. We will remain on the streets," he said.
Speaking about the recent law-and-order situation, Ishraque praised law enforcement agencies for their handling of unrest and what he described as attempts to create political instability during recent labour protests.
Regarding the hartal called by the Awami League, he said the programme would have little impact.
"The people of Bangladesh have rejected the Awami League, a party of murderers, autocrats and fascists. The party is effectively banned. Following the 2024 mass uprising and in view of the upcoming trials over genocide, the courts will decide whether the Awami League will be allowed to continue political activities under that name," he said.
Describing the party's recent activities as acts of terrorism, Ishraque alleged that its members operating from abroad were orchestrating sporadic acts of sabotage. He said the activities would bring them no political gains.
Pointing to traffic congestion in the capital on Tuesday morning, he said the general public was not voluntarily observing the hartal.
Ishraque added that the government was making every effort to restore normalcy to the law-and-order situation and address the challenges through political initiatives. He said steps were also being taken to bring those involved in covert attacks and sabotage to justice.
State Minister for Fisheries and Livestock Sultan Salauddin Tuku, Dhaka Deputy Commissioner Farida Khanom and others were present at the meeting.

item.title: Your home could be hiding more air pollutants than you realize
item.description:
A home may offer shelter from outdoor pollution, but the air inside is not always free from harmful pollutants. Everyday household activities and materials, including cooking fumes, mosquito coils, cleaning chemicals, substances released from furniture, and mold growing on damp walls, can all contribute to indoor air pollution.
As people spend a significant part of their day indoors, their exposure to these pollutants can be considerable. Therefore, keeping a home clean also means paying attention to indoor air quality.
The kitchen is one of the major sources of indoor air pollution. Cooking with gas stoves can release pollutants such as nitrogen dioxide. In addition, frying food in excessively heated oil can release fine particles into the air. Using wood, coal, or other solid fuels can produce even more smoke.
Without proper ventilation, these pollutants can accumulate indoors. Prolonged exposure to polluted air may increase the risk of respiratory problems.
To reduce these risks, use an exhaust fan while cooking, keep windows open when safe to do so, and ensure adequate ventilation in the kitchen.
Floor cleaners, glass cleaners, air fresheners, and scented sprays are commonly used to keep homes clean. However, these products can release volatile organic compounds (VOCs) into the air.
Exposure to certain chemicals may cause eye and nose irritation, headaches, and breathing difficulties.
To minimize these risks, avoid using more sprays than necessary. Where possible, apply sprays to a cleaning cloth rather than dispersing them directly into the air. Ensure proper ventilation after cleaning and never mix different cleaning products, as this can produce dangerous gases.
Certain chemicals used in sofas, mattresses, carpets, curtains, and foam-based products can gradually enter household dust and indoor air. Researchers are also studying the potential health risks associated with certain flame-retardant chemicals used in these products.
When purchasing new furniture, it is advisable to check the materials and chemicals used in its production.
Regularly wipe furniture with a damp cloth to remove dust. Where possible, use a vacuum cleaner equipped with a high-efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filter, which can help reduce household dust.
The cookware used at home also requires attention. If the coating of a non-stick pan becomes scratched or damaged, it is better to replace it. Avoid overheating such cookware as well.
Using wooden or other suitable soft utensils while cooking can help prevent scratches on the coating.
Certain plastic containers may release chemicals into food under specific conditions. Therefore, it is better to use microwave-safe glass or ceramic containers when heating food. Always check whether a plastic container is suitable for heating food before using it.
Mold can grow on walls, ceilings, cupboards, and furniture when they remain damp for extended periods. Exposure to mold may worsen allergy symptoms, cause eye and nose irritation, and increase the risk of respiratory problems.
Such issues are more common in poorly ventilated spaces.
To reduce the risk, remove excess moisture after cooking and bathing. Drying clothes outdoors where possible and controlling indoor humidity are also important.
If mold appears on walls or furniture, simply cleaning the visible surface may not be enough. The source of moisture must also be identified and addressed.
Maintaining healthy indoor air does not always require major changes. A few simple habits can help reduce pollution inside the home:
Keeping a home clean is not just about having spotless floors or neatly arranged furniture. The air inside should also be healthy. Alongside protecting ourselves from outdoor pollution, identifying and addressing indoor pollution sources can play an important role in safeguarding the health of ourselves and our families.

item.title: Can drinking tea lower your risk of heart disease?
item.description:
Many people start their mornings with a cup of tea, often returning to it several times throughout the day. Besides helping people feel refreshed, regular and moderate tea consumption may also benefit heart health.
A new study has found that regular tea drinkers have an 11% lower risk of heart and blood vessel-related diseases compared to those who do not drink tea.
The findings also suggest that tea may help reduce the risk of stroke and blood clots. However, its potential health benefits may depend on the type of tea, its temperature, and the amount consumed.
The study followed 485,934 adults in China over nine years. It found that moderately brewed black tea served warm may be beneficial for heart health.
People who combined tea drinking with healthy habits, such as avoiding smoking and exercising regularly, had the lowest risk of heart disease.
However, the findings also indicated that tea might offer some degree of protection even for smokers.
Jean Copeland, a clinical dietitian at the Heart and Vascular Center of Dartmouth Hitchcock Medical Center, said tea cannot provide the same level of protection as avoiding smoking. However, it may offer some benefits to smokers.
She noted that the findings provide important insights into the potential health benefits of tea.
Tea is a good source of catechins, a type of flavonoid with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties. These compounds may help maintain healthy blood circulation and lower the risk of heart disease.
Some studies have also linked compounds found in tea to a reduced risk of memory decline.
According to dietitian Jean Copeland, steeping tea leaves in water for two to three minutes is enough to release their antioxidants. Leaving tea to steep for longer does not necessarily increase its health benefits. Instead, it may make the tea bitter and negatively affect its catechin content.
The study found a more consistent positive association between black tea consumption and heart health than with green tea.
Previous research has also suggested that unsweetened black and green tea may help lower cholesterol levels and regulate blood pressure.
Grace Derocha, a registered dietitian based in Detroit and a spokesperson for the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, said black tea contains an antioxidant called theaflavin, which may positively influence inflammation and fat metabolism.
However, she cautioned against concluding that black tea is healthier than green tea. Both varieties contain beneficial plant compounds and may support heart health.
Besides the type and strength of tea, its temperature may also affect health.
Several studies have linked drinking excessively hot tea to an increased risk of oesophageal and stomach cancers. Very hot beverages can repeatedly damage the lining of the oesophagus through heat exposure.
The study found some positive associations with heart health among people who drank warm or room-temperature tea. However, this does not mean that drinking six to eight cups daily will provide the same benefits to everyone.
According to cardiologist Anam Wahid, drinking ordinary tea in moderation may be beneficial, but excessively hot tea should be avoided. Drinking more tea does not necessarily mean gaining greater health benefits.
The study participants reported their own tea consumption, and the sizes of their cups varied. As a result, researchers could not establish an exact amount of tea that would provide the greatest heart health benefits.
Dietitian Grace Derocha said drinking more tea does not necessarily offer greater protection. Excessive caffeine intake can also disrupt sleep.
Some previous studies have found positive health associations with drinking two to four cups of tea daily.
What people add to their tea also matters. Adding sugar increases the drink's calorie content, making unsweetened tea a healthier option. Lemon juice, mint leaves, or cinnamon can be used to enhance its flavor instead.
Overall, moderate tea consumption may support heart health. However, it should never be considered a substitute for quitting smoking, exercising regularly, maintaining a balanced diet, or following medical advice.
Those who enjoy tea should avoid drinking it excessively hot and consider their individual caffeine tolerance when deciding how much to consume.

item.title: Chastity, trauma and the subjugation of women
item.description:
Although rape remains one of the most pressing social issues in our country, how extensively has this issue been explored in literature?
Literature reflects human happiness, sorrows, love, frustration, struggle, and the other realities of life, but sexual violence such as rape is often explored less extensively due to social and cultural sensitivities. However, 10,000 Ebang Aro Ekti Dhorshon (2003), a novel by Humayun Azad offers a direct and forthright portrayal of the suffering and social position of rape survivors as well as the stigma and pressure they face.
The novel also explores the underlying causes behind the increasing prevalence of rape in society, presenting these issues openly and without euphemism.
In the story, we see a very young, beautiful, and lively girl, Mayna. One afternoon, a group of perverts attacks and repeatedly rapes her. Mayna’s rejection hurts their ego, so they resort to revenge. Through their conversations, we acknowledge how fearless and arrogant they are about committing such a crime because they hold power within society.
Here, the author somewhat reveals the mindset of the perpetrators, which resonates with Peggy Reeves Sanday’s analysis of rape. Sanday argues that rape is not merely a sexual act; rather, it can function as an instrument of power, control, and the domination of women. As she also states, “Sexual violence is one of the ways in which men remind themselves that they are superior” (The Socio-Cultural Context of Rape: A Cross-Cultural Study, 1981).
When Mayna is found severely wounded, a wail of anguish spreads among the crowd around her: “Who ruined the girl?”
It seems as if the loss of her chastity was a far greater injury than the physical trauma she endured. After regaining some consciousness, she started to thrash about, so they assumed that Mayna may have been possessed by an evil spirit. Her mother seems somewhat relieved by hearing this; it is preferable to her to believe that Mayna has been possessed rather than “ruined” by rape.
As the story unfolds, we see her mother’s apprehension about whether anyone would marry her daughter.
This brings to mind the famous observation of pioneering feminist Mary Wollstonecraft: “It is the eye of man that they have been taught to dread” (A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, 1792).
Her statement shows that society has conditioned women to become more concerned with their acceptability in the eyes of men than with their own personal well-being.
Gradually, Mayna wants to return to normal life and leave everything behind. However, society becomes an obstacle here. Humiliation and condemnation made her life extremely distressing.
Rape is not merely a crime committed against a woman’s body; society’s response can often reproduce the violence and trauma on the survivor.
At the same time, the novel exposes one of the harsh realities of our society; while perpetrators of rape can live fearlessly and unrestrained, the victims have to struggle at every step.
Yet, this reality should have been exactly the opposite; the perpetrator should face condemnation for his crime, while the survivor should receive protection, dignity, and support.
One of the most striking aspects of the novel is how it exposes the ways in which women are pushed into subordinate social positions. In the story, the emergence of a few hypocritical religious preachers gradually undermined the social position of women. Invoking religion, they began devising ways to confine girls to their homes, and many parents stopped sending their daughters to school by their propaganda.
Moreover, these hypocritical religious leaders portray women as objects of contempt, sources of sin, and inferior beings. Such misogynist values gradually seep into society like a slow poison.
As a result, society begins to point its finger at the rape survivor rather than the perpetrator and ultimately, to despise her more than the man who committed the crime.
At a large religious gathering, the Maulana continues his sermon before a huge crowd: “O believing brothers, the world has become filled with sin. At the root of this sin are two chief devils; one of them is the woman... Brothers, do not trust women, just as you would not trust the devil...” The Maulana also says, “Men are the masters of women. Allah has created men far superior to women. Allah created women for men. They were created from the crooked rib of Adam. Had men not needed them, Allah would not have created women. Therefore, women should remain under the authority of men.”
In this way, the hypocritical Maulana continues to demean women in the name of religion, replacing the true teachings of religion with misogynist statements in its name.
However, the ordinary villagers often accept these claims without questioning or critically examining them. Some school-going girls listen to the sermon and are left stunned:
Faju says, “Did you hear that, buddy? Apparently, we are devils?”
Fuli replies, “Who knows how many more insults we have to endure? It seems we were born just to be abused.”
From these brief exchanges, we can understand that a culture of openly spreading misogyny is not new. The girls are agitated, yet they have no power to protest, as if society has decided that being born a woman means living a life marked by humiliation and degradation.
The way religious leaders often compel women to remain subordinate and reinforce the notion of women as the property of men, Judith Butler demonstrates in her influential book “Who’s Afraid of Gender?" Butler argues religious discourse does not merely shape individuals’ understanding of gender; it can also play a role in defining what are considered “natural” roles for men and women, establishing the moral legitimacy of those roles, and ultimately incorporating them into broader political and social structures.
This is evident not only in the literature but also in the society we live in. Even today, a few self-proclaimed religious figures ignore women's dignity in religion and continue to make hateful remarks about women at religious gatherings.
Moreover, with the influence of social media, such misogynistic ideas are spreading rapidly nowadays. For instance, hateful sermons are not limited to religious assemblies; they are recorded and widely spreading on social media. Alarmingly, some social media pages promote patriarchal gender norms and even normalize child marriage.
In the name of religion, they seek to deprive women of their right to education and other rights, confine them within the four walls of their homes, and construct the notions of the “ideal woman” and the “immoral woman.” A woman who is self-sacrificing and obedient, conforms to social norms, and dresses according to socially accepted standards of modesty is portrayed as the “ideal woman.” In contrast, educated, career-oriented, and independent women are portrayed as “selfish.” These narratives help legitimize violence against women. Unfortunately, ordinary people are unwittingly swallowing these toxic ideologies.
Mayna doesn't judge herself by the decadent society's values, nor does she emotionally break down. She asked, Is she really responsible for what happened to her?
Her voice challenges the deep-rooted notion of victim-blaming and compels readers to understand that the victim is not responsible for the crime; rather, the responsibility lies with the perpetrator and the rotten social system that fosters criminal mentality and nurtures criminals. She doesn’t confine herself to shame, humiliation, or inferiority. With the support of her well-wishers, she finds happiness again. One day, she returns to her school, facing rejection but firmly expresses her desire to continue her study.
Here, the author presents Mayna as an exceptional character and offers a lesson in courage and inspiration for ordinary women.
Mayna didn’t demand justice for the wrong done to her. Her silence becomes a protest against a society and justice system that have repeatedly failed women like her. When the village dignitaries approach her to identify the perpetrators and assure her that action will be taken against them.
But Mayna turns them away and asks how many of the other rape survivors in the village have actually received justice. Her question extends beyond her own experience, exposing a larger reality in which seeking justice often brings little hope of receiving it. Through its fictional setting and characters, the story thus offers a powerful critique of the culture of impunity that exists in reality.
Mayna’s experience is not merely a fictional tragedy; it is the mirror of broader social and institutional reality. In Bangladesh, delayed justice and weak enforcement of laws are responsible for emboldening perpetrators to act with impunity and perpetuating violence. According to official data from the High Court, over 35,000 cases of violence had remained pending for more than five years.
In this sense, 10,000, Ebang Aro Ekti Dhorshon is not just a novel but rather a reflection of our society, where injustice persists through institutional failure and social indifference. At the same time, through Mayna’s resilience, the novel offers courage and inspiration to women who face oppression.
Ultimately, the story transforms Mayna’s personal struggle into a broader indictment of a society that fails to ensure justice for its vulnerable members.
Rufaiya Zia Nuha is an M.A. student at the Department of World Religions and Culture, University of Dhaka

item.title: M John Harrison becomes the first science fiction writer to win the Booker Prize
item.description:
British author M John Harrison, 81, has won the 2026 Booker Prize for his post-apocalyptic novel The End of Everything , becoming the oldest recipient in the award’s history and the first science fiction writer to win the prestigious literary honor.
Harrison received the £50,000 prize and trophy at a ceremony held at Old Billingsgate in London on Monday, 9 November. He overtook Margaret Atwood, who was 79 when she jointly won the award in 2019 for The Testaments .
The Booker Prize judging panel unanimously selected The End of Everything after a day of discussions among the six shortlisted novels. Mary Beard, chair of the judges, described it as a book that challenges readers while offering an unexpected sense of optimism.
The novel, published by Serpent’s Tail, is set on the Kent coast a few decades in the future, following an unexplained disaster. It centers on Phillip Tennent and his ageing aunt Marnie as they struggle to survive amid the presence of mysterious, shape-shifting beings known as the iGhetti.
At 198 pages, it was the shortest novel on this year's shortlist and Harrison's first Booker Prize nomination.
Gaby Wood, chief executive of the Booker Prize Foundation, said previous winners had explored science fiction, but Harrison was the first winner to emerge from the established science fiction community. She described the victory as a historic achievement for a writer whose career spans six decades.
Harrison, born in Rugby, Warwickshire, in 1945, began publishing stories in 1965. His previous works include Climbers , which won the Boardman Tasker Prize for Mountain Literature in 1989; Nova Swing , which received the Arthur C Clarke Award in 2007; and The Sunken Land Begins to Rise Again , which won the Goldsmiths Prize in 2020.
The 2026 shortlist also included The Disappearers by Marlon James, Black Bag by Luke Kennard, May We Feed the King by Rebecca Perry, The Things We Never Say by Elizabeth Strout and John of John by Douglas Stuart. Each shortlisted author received £2,500.
The win also marks the first Booker Prize victory for Harrison's publisher, Serpent’s Tail, an imprint of Profile Books, following five previous nominations.
The Booker Prize recognizes the best work of long-form fiction written in English and published in the United Kingdom or Ireland.

item.title: grocery store
item.description:
i went to the grocery store today
with a fridge fully stocked.
walked through the aisles with my hands losing grip of the trolley,
fingers slipping off despite the sterile, air-conditioned walls.
like how yours slipped off mine despite our content, contained world.
one that i could pack up in a lunchbox and send away for the day
without fear, as it would always come back.
always be here.
i walked past the plastic-wrapped bouquets of flowers
without instantly pointing to them like a reflex arc;
muscle memory.
poster relationship.
boy meets girl, girl meets boy.
the rest i’ve heard you say a couple hundred times
before we went to bed,
with your eyes lit up, my cheeks flushed red
like i hadn’t lived it all out.
i could’ve picked some up.
it’s not that i can’t get myself flowers.
not like my vase has been filled in quite some time.
but i didn’t. i don’t.
it’s that the smell reminds me of you
and i just can’t quite bring myself
to let that scent linger again.
exactly why i’m wearing this fake, put-together outfit
and not my? your big maroon t-shirt
that i’d wear to run errands.
can’t let that scent linger again.
i stopped by the fruits.
i don’t need any, there’s way too many at home.
i usually slice the pears and sprinkle them with beet lobon,
have them as an afternoon snack.
but you wouldn’t put a fruit near your mouth.
the texture weirds you out.
so i stood there,
grabbing one of each.
apples, oranges, grapes, pineapples.
trying to understand where you came from,
but i’d never get it.
fruits are nature’s candy.
so sweet, how can someone not like them?
but you wouldn’t get that.
walked past the junk food.
now that’s what i probably would end up eating anyway.
that and bhaat and bhorta.
something to sustain me, something to make me happy,
something to have when my missing appetite
decides to show up.
i grabbed a couple of things, paid and left.
walked home safely, but you don’t know that.
i haven’t called you to say that in some time.
i think you’d like to know.
or maybe you wouldn’t.
but i don’t let myself think too much these days,
so i don’t really know.
i unpacked my shopping bag,
immediately put the ice cream in the freezer.
it’s funny how it stood on a cone
when i’m such an advocate for cups.
it’s funnier how i got vanilla when i like chocolate.
you creep up on me, don’t you?
how i wish we could be something more.
something more than a friendship,
but something less than a relationship.
you’re too special for a term
that’s interchangeable with others.
but that’s the best we could do
when neither being together felt right,
nor did being strangers.
i stared at the chips i got.
four of them, electric blue “magic masala”.
i like the green ones.
they were in stock.
but these felt better.
felt closer to you when i got them.
what even is close anymore?
i’ve heard you breathe in your sleep,
heard your heart beat while i lay on your chest.
but now this is what feels closer
than when i counted the moles on your body.
isn’t that something?
i put the last of the groceries away.
the fridge is full.
the freezer is cold.
the flowers are still on the shelf
and the maroon shirt is still at the back of my closet.
i wonder if you went grocery shopping today,
if you picked up the green ones,
if you got chocolate,
if you thought of me at all.
i wonder if i’ll end up forgetting my favourite flavours,
if they’ll change without me realising it.
i wonder if i’ll ever understand where i end
and where you begin.
i wonder if you’ll do the same.
Marissa Manal Waiz is a Dhaka-based writer who recently completed her A-Levels.

item.title: Saltwater
item.description:
Why do I break open before you,
spill salt into your palms,
when I know you will not hold me?
Perhaps for a fleeting moment—
but soon your hands drown,
and I am forced to vanish,
slipping into the dark,
into a dream that gnaws at my ribs,
into a memory so violent in its beauty
that it never truly existed.
Nubisha Rabya Topote, an XI-grade student at Holy Cross College, is a poet and writer who finds inspiration in the world around her.

item.title: Home minister: Law and order better than last year
item.description:
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed has claimed that the country's law and order situation is better than it was last year, citing a decline of around 300 in the number of murders during the same period.
Speaking in the parliament on Tuesday, he urged lawmakers to assess the security situation by comparing crime statistics year on year rather than drawing conclusions from isolated incidents such as crude bomb explosions and arson attacks.
Responding to concerns raised by Opposition Leader Shafiqur Rahman and Chief Whip Nahid Islam during the fourth session of the 13th parliament, the minister said seven crude bomb explosions had been reported across the country in recent days. Law enforcement agencies had taken action, arresting several suspects.
Referring to a cocktail explosion on a vehicle near Dhaka University's Business Faculty, he said such incidents did not indicate a nationwide deterioration in law and order. Setting fire to abandoned vehicles at night or in the early morning also did not necessarily mean the political situation had become unstable.
Ahmed alleged that ousted Awami League-linked forces were attempting to create unrest, possibly with support from across the border. The government was investigating those involved and their sources of support, he said.
He also alleged that attempts to destabilise the garment sector had been planned abroad with local support, but the government had thwarted them. Law enforcement agencies had handled the unrest with restraint, while police, industrial police and Border Guard Bangladesh were working together to maintain security in industrial areas.
Assuring factory owners, investors and international buyers, the minister said the government would maintain a stable, industry-friendly environment and take firm action against attempts to disrupt production and exports.
Citing police website data, Ahmed said the number of murders had fallen by around 300 compared with the same period last year. He pledged to present detailed crime statistics in parliament on Wednesday so that the figures could be independently verified.

item.title: Khulna resident wins household appliances after buying Walton Fridge
item.description:
A refrigerator purchase turned into an extraordinary experience for Shatarupa Biswas, a resident of Dakbangla in Khulna, as she received a houseful of electronic appliances for free under Walton’s ongoing ‘Houseful Offer’ as part of its Digital Campaign Season-25.
Shatarupa and her family were overjoyed to receive a wide range of Walton products, including another refrigerator, an air conditioner, a smart television, a washing machine, a microwave oven, a gas hob, a rice cooker, a blender, a ceiling fan, a rechargeable fan, lights, a room heater, a smartphone and a soundbar.
Popular film actor Amin Khan and model-actress Sadia Ayman formally handed over the gifts to Shatarupa at a colourful ceremony held at Shaheed Hadis Park in Khulna city on Monday (November 9, 2026).
Organized by Walton Plaza’s Dakbangla branch, the event drew enthusiastic crowds from different parts of the city, creating a festive atmosphere as people gathered to witness the handover of the gifts.
Among others, Walton Plaza managing director Mohammad Rayhan, head of sales MM Nazmul Hasan, Walton chief marketing officer Zoheb Ahmed, Walton Plaza head of HRM Faysal Wahid, and sales representatives and officials of Walton Plaza’s Khulna region attended the ceremony.
Speaking at the event, Walton officials said the company launched its nationwide ‘Digital Campaign Season-25’ on October 17, ahead of the winter season, offering customers a host of attractive benefits.
Under the campaign’s special ‘Walton Houseful Offer’, customers purchasing refrigerators, televisions, air conditioners, washing machines or BLDC fans from any Walton Plaza or authorized distributor showroom across the country have the opportunity to win a houseful of electronic appliances for free upon completing digital registration.
The campaign, which will continue until December 31, 2026, also offers opportunities to win overseas trips, cashback and a range of guaranteed gifts.
Shatarupa recently purchased a refrigerator from Walton Plaza’s Dakbangla branch in Khulna.
Following the purchase, her details, including her name, mobile phone number and the refrigerator’s barcode number, were registered in Walton’s digital system.
Shortly afterwards, she received an SMS on her registered mobile number informing her that she had won a houseful of free electronic appliances under the ‘Walton Houseful Offer’.
Recalling the moment at the handover ceremony, Shatarupa said she initially could hardly believe the message.
“I chose Walton because its refrigerators are good in quality, attractive in design and affordable. I never imagined that buying a fridge would bring such a wonderful surprise for my family,” she added.
Walton has been developing a comprehensive ‘Digital Customer Database’ to make its after-sales services faster, more efficient and automated.
Through the system, customers’ purchase and product information are securely stored on Walton’s own servers, enabling them to receive warranty services from any Walton service centre across Bangladesh, even if they lose their physical warranty cards.
Walton has been conducting its digital campaigns to encourage customers to participate in the registration process while enhancing customer convenience and strengthening its after-sales service network.

item.title: Southeast Bank, CliniCall launch co-branded healthcare card
item.description:
Southeast Bank PLC. and CliniCall Limited signed an agreement to launch a co-branded healthcare card.
The card combines everyday banking and digital healthcare benefits in a single Visa card.
It extends the value of a payment card beyond financial transactions.
Cardholders can use healthcare benefits simply by presenting their card at participating healthcare facilities.
Md Khalid Mahmood Khan, managing director of Southeast Bank PLC, and Malik Talha Ismail Bari, chairman of CliniCall Limited jointly inaugurated the cards at a ceremony in Dhaka.
Abidur Rahman Chowdhury, additional managing director of Southeast Bank PLC, Md Mahbub Alam, additional managing director of Southeast Bank PLC, Md Sekander-E-Azam, deputy managing director of Southeast Bank PLC, and Parvez Ahmad, co-founder & COO, CliniCall Limited, Saad M Milkan, head of business, CliniCall, Limited along with other senior officials from both the organizations were also present.
Cardholders will receive unlimited 24/7 audio and video doctor consultations, 365 days a year. Benefits also include hospital cashback, cashback on doctor visits, insurance coverage, and discounts up to 40% at more than 300 partner hospitals nationwide.
All benefits are subject to applicable terms and conditions. Out-of-pocket spending accounts for nearly 70% of total health expenditure in Bangladesh, and many families delay care because of cost or limited access to doctors.
The card addresses this by putting a doctor within reach at any hour and reducing the cost of hospital care. It also adds financial protection through insurance.

item.title: Three DB men injured during anti-drug drive at Kushtia Govt College
item.description:
Three members of the District Detective Branch (DB) of police were injured in an attack while conducting an anti-drug operation on the campus of Kushtia Government College on Tuesday night.
The injured were identified as DB Sub-Inspectors Johnny and Jihad, and Constable Imran.
They received treatment at Kushtia General Hospital after the incident. However, police described the incident as a "misunderstanding".
The incident took place on the college campus around 9:00pm on Tuesday.
According to sources, a DB team went to the college campus to conduct an anti-drug operation when an altercation took place and the police personnel came under attack.
They were later rescued and taken to Kushtia General Hospital for treatment.
At around 9:30pm, the three officers were seen receiving treatment at the hospital's emergency department. They left after receiving initial medical care.
Dr Iqbal Hasan, Resident Medical Officer (RMO) of Kushtia General Hospital, said the police officers had received treatment, but their names were not recorded in the hospital's official register.
Police have yet to disclose who was involved in the incident or what led to it.
Contacted over the incident, Kushtia Superintendent of Police Aminul Islam said he was not fully aware of the details.
"My officers went there. I will be able to provide more information once they return," he said.

item.title: Baishnab poet Radha Raman's 111th death anniversary observed
item.description:
The 111th death anniversary of renowned Baishnab poet, lyricist and composer Radha Raman Dutta observed with a Dhamail festival and cultural programmes in Sunamganj yesterday.
Born in 1833 at Keshabpur village in Jagannathpur upazila of the district, Dutta composed more than 3,000 songs, according to various researchers.
His timeless compositions, including 'Bhramar Koio Giya' and 'Murshid Boli Nouka Chharo', remain an integral part of Bengali folk music.
His songs explore devotion, spirituality, human values, patriotism and religious harmony. His Dhamail compositions are particularly popular in the Sylhet region.
Dutta died on November 10, 1915. Around 1,050 of his songs have, so far, been preserved digitally.
District Shilpakala Academy Cultural Officer Ahmed Manjurul Haque Chowdhury Pavel said Dutta's creations were an invaluable treasure of Bengali folk literature but expressed concern over the distortion of his original lyrics and melodies.
He stressed the need for proper preservation and authentic practice of the poet's songs.
Local cultural activists also called for the construction of a Radha Raman Complex at his birthplace to preserve his legacy. Although the Bangladesh Shilpakala Academy took an initiative in this regard, the project has yet to be implemented.
The District Shilpakala Academy and local cultural organisations jointly organised the Dhamail festival and cultural programmes marking the anniversary.

item.title: Bapex inspects Inani gas site
item.description:
A 15-member team from Bangladesh Petroleum Exploration and Production Company Ltd (Bapex) inspected a gas seepage site in Inani, Ukhia, Cox’s Bazar, on Tuesday, where gas has been burning continuously for the past 15 days.
Following an initial assessment, the team said Bapex’s senior authorities would decide whether the fire could be safely extinguished and whether the gas could be extracted commercially.
The team visited the site in the morning and examined the point of gas emission, soil structure, gas flow and surrounding environment. Representatives of the local administration were also present.
Bapex geologist Nasir Uddin, a member of the team, said: “We have completed 15 days of observation and preliminary assessment. Bapex’s senior authorities will now decide how to safely extinguish the fire and whether commercial gas extraction is feasible.”
He said the team had collected data on the nature and pressure of the gas, the sustainability of the flow and potential reserves. Further technical tests may be conducted if necessary before deciding on the next steps.
Local residents, including Jasim Uddin, Mohammad Ali and Tarek Ullah, said the continuous burning had initially caused panic, but the site was now attracting growing numbers of curious visitors every day.
They called for a permanent solution to bring the fire under control and ensure the safety of the surrounding area.
Experts say the discovery of natural gas does not mean it can be immediately extracted or that the fire can be extinguished without proper assessment. Geological and engineering tests are needed to determine the volume of reserves, pressure, quality and commercial viability before any extraction plan is drawn up.
Local residents hope that if sufficient reserves are confirmed in Inani, the discovery could open up new prospects for the country's energy sector.
Meanwhile, security has been tightened around the site, and people have been advised to maintain a safe distance.

item.title: Why are the malls empty?
item.description:
The most revealing feature of Dhaka’s struggling shopping malls is not the number of closed shutters, but the hesitation behind them. A market may have merchandise on its shelves, staff waiting behind counters and discounts displayed, yet customers can walk past.
The decline in activity at established destinations such as Eastern Plaza, Eastern Mallika, Mouchak Market, Police Plaza, and Shah Ali Plaza, alongside the closure of Karnaphuli Garden City, invites a larger question: What happens when consumers lose not only the capacity to spend, but also the confidence to do so?
It is easy to explain the retreat by pointing to online shopping and the arrival of newer commercial complexes. Both have altered the retail landscape. Digital platforms allow customers to compare prices, browse products and arrange delivery without negotiating Dhaka’s traffic.
Modern malls offer facilities that older markets may lack. Yet these changes explain where people shop, not necessarily why they are buying less.
When traders across different locations report falling sales, vacant shops, and difficulty meeting rent and salaries, the issue cannot be reduced to a competition between physical and digital stores. It points to a weakening of demand across the marketplace.
The pressure begins in the household budget. Food, housing, transport, education, healthcare, and utility bills claim first place because they cannot easily be postponed.
Clothing, cosmetics, shoes, jewellery and household upgrades come later. When the cost of essentials rises faster than income, discretionary purchases become the first casualties.
Families may continue to buy what they need, but they buy less frequently, choose cheaper alternatives, repair rather than replace, or simply wait. The absence of a customer in a shop may therefore represent a decision made long before that person reaches the market: The household has already decided that the purchase can no longer be justified.
This is the difference between having money and having disposable income. A person may receive the same salary as before and still feel poorer because that salary commands fewer goods and services.
Retailers face the reverse side of the same squeeze. Imported products become more expensive, while rent, electricity, wages, and service charges add to operating costs.
A shopkeeper cannot indefinitely absorb these increases. Prices rise, but customers whose incomes have not kept pace resist them. Traders are caught between costs they cannot control and buyers who cannot afford the prices required to cover those costs. Offering a discount may attract attention, but it cannot solve a structural loss of purchasing power.
The psychology of this retreat deserves as much attention as its arithmetic. Consumers do not make every decision by comparing prices and calculating immediate utility. They also respond to fear, expectations, habits, and the possibility of future hardship.
A family uncertain about employment, medical expenses, or next month’s bills may avoid spending even when it has some money left. Savings become a buffer against risks that feel increasingly difficult to predict. The pleasure of buying something new competes with the reassurance of keeping cash available. In uncertain times, reassurance often wins.
Behavioural economics offers a useful explanation. Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky’s prospect theory argues that people assess outcomes relative to a reference point and that losses can carry greater psychological weight than equivalent gains.
Their memorable formulation, “losses loom larger than gains,” helps explain why a consumer may experience spending as a potential loss of security rather than simply an exchange of money for a product.
The prospect of enjoying a new pair of shoes may seem modest beside the fear of being unable to meet an unexpected expense. The decision not to buy is then not evidence of indifference to consumption; it is a response to perceived vulnerability.
Another relevant concept is loss aversion, which can make consumers particularly sensitive to price increases. A product that once cost Tk 1,000 but now costs Tk 1,400 is not experienced merely as a new market price. The increase can feel like a loss of purchasing power, especially when wages remain unchanged.
Even if the item is still affordable in absolute terms, the buyer may resent paying more and postpone the purchase. Repeated price shocks can gradually reset expectations. Consumers begin to regard older spending habits as excessive and develop a more restrictive idea of what is necessary.
Richard Thaler’s work on behavioural economics also challenges the assumption that people behave like perfectly rational economic actors. His distinction between “econs” and “humans” captures the gap between theoretical decision-makers and actual people, whose choices are shaped by context and emotion.
A shopper may respond to a discount, but may also avoid a purchase because the household budget feels fragile. A retailer who assumes that lower prices alone will restore demand may misunderstand the customer’s real calculation.
The consumer is not simply asking whether an item is cheaper today; the consumer is asking whether buying it will create anxiety tomorrow.
There are, of course, problems within the retail sector itself. Some older shopping complexes have failed to maintain facilities or adapt to changing expectations. Poor ventilation, inactive escalators, neglected common areas, limited product variety, and weak customer service can make a visit less attractive. Buyers increasingly expect convenient payment options, reliable products, transparent prices, and the ability to compare alternatives.
A mall that once enjoyed prestige cannot depend indefinitely on its history. The difficulties of older complexes therefore reflect both an economic squeeze and a failure by some businesses and property managers to renew the shopping experience.
The damage does not stop at the shop counter. Retail connects importers, manufacturers, wholesalers, transport operators, delivery workers, landlords, and employees. When sales decline, retailers reduce orders.
Suppliers carry less stock, manufacturers may cut production, and businesses under pressure may reduce staff or delay investment. Lost jobs and lower incomes then weaken demand further.
A decline in consumption can thus become a cycle: Households spend less, businesses earn less, employment becomes less secure, and households become even more cautious. Empty corridors are only the visible part of a much wider chain.
This is why the condition of shopping malls should not be dismissed as nostalgia for an older style of shopping.
Karnaphuli Garden City’s closure is a reminder that commercial property cannot survive on its location or reputation alone. Nor should every struggling market be treated as proof that consumers have moved online.
The more important question is whether people across income groups have enough confidence and financial room to participate in ordinary consumption. A transfer of purchases from a physical shop to a website is a change in channel. A household abandoning purchases altogether is a sign of economic contraction.
Policy must therefore address the conditions that shape consumer confidence. Controlling inflation, creating secure employment, protecting real wages, ensuring fair competition, and reducing the burden of essential services are not merely social objectives; they are foundations of a functioning domestic market.
Reliable information and predictable economic management also matter because uncertainty influences spending decisions. Retailers, for their part, must improve facilities, use digital channels intelligently, maintain transparent pricing, and respond to customers with different budgets.
Neither public policy nor commercial innovation can guarantee success for every shop, but both can help create an environment in which demand has room to recover.
The quietness of Dhaka’s shopping malls is ultimately a story about the relationship between income, expectation, and trust in the future. People do not stop wanting attractive clothes, comfortable homes, or small pleasures simply because a market has changed.
They stop buying when the cost of those pleasures appears too high against the risks they face. Behind a vacant shop is a household making choices about food, rent, tuition, medicine, and the next uncertain month.
When ordinary purchases begin to feel financially dangerous, the crisis belongs not only to retailers. It belongs to an economy whose consumers are losing the freedom to spend.
HM Nazmul Alam is an academic, journalist, and political analyst based in Dhaka, Bangladesh. Currently he is teaching at IUBAT.

item.title: Who is Jensen Huang and why the Nvidia CEO scandal is such a huge deal
item.description:
In terms of corporate fallout, what has happened at Nvidia has been huge.
The company, seen as the darling of the AI era, has lost hundreds of billions of dollars in market value since it was revealed that its chief executive, Jensen Huang, had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.
Nvidia and Mr Huang are now being sued, accused of ⁠defrauding shareholders by concealing the affair.
Nvidia has both benefited from and brought about the global AI revolution.
And, as CEOs go, few are as synonymous with a company as Jensen Huang.
“Treating this simply as a sex scandal misses the point,” technology strategist Josh Kennedy-White says.
“The real issue is whether personal access to one of the world’s most strategically important executives became a channel for intelligence gathering or influence.”
So how did we get here?
Born in Taiwan, Mr Huang moved to the US at the age of nine and, at some point, naturalized as a US citizen.
At 17, he attended university in Oregon, where he met his wife Lori Mills, who was two years his senior.
Both were studying electrical engineering, and Mr Huang has previously recounted using the pick-up line: “Do you wanna see my homework?”
They had weekly study dates, became lab partners and, five years later, married.
In an interview with a magazine at his alma mater in 2013, he described how his wife’s support has always been unconditional.
“Ever since I was 18, she was there believing in me and knowing I could do it. Even when I had self-doubts, she didn’t,” he said.
The two went on to have two children, Spencer and Madison Huang, who both now hold executive roles at Nvidia.
In 1993, at a diner in San Jose, Mr Huang met with Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, fellow engineers he had worked with in the chip industry since the late 1980s.
They came up with Nvidia, starting with just $40,000 in capital. In order to incorporate the business, the three founders gave $200 each.
Originally, gaming was the focus. The founders believed the PC gaming market was set to grow and would need more powerful graphics processing.
After a near business-ending initial failure, Nvidia invented what is regarded as the world’s first Graphics Processing Unit in 1999. The chips could make advanced computer graphics, allowing for advanced 3D environments in video games and perform huge numbers of calculations in parallel.
It was not long before developers realized their uses could go far beyond gaming.
“We created the world’s first programmable accelerator,” Mr Huang said in 2023.
“And the benefit of an accelerator is whatever you designed it to do, it does it incredibly efficiently.”
And so, the era of modern AI was born.
Nvidia’s chips, by all accounts, are unparalleled. They are so hot, companies struggle to get their hands on them, and the metrics of Nvidia’s growth are dizzying.
To give you a sense of some of the numbers: Its shares have increased some 477,000% since listing in 1999; almost five-fold in the past five years.
For Mr Huang, who is estimated to own about 3.5% of the company, his wealth has skyrocketed.
According to Forbes, he was worth $2 billion in 2017 — and now, about $154 billion, putting him in the top 10 wealthiest people in the world.
With his trademark leather jackets and high-profile product launches, Mr Huang is omnipresent at Nvidia.
Its website lists him as co-founder, president, chief executive officer and a member of the board of directors.
“He is Nvidia. [He] clearly sets the long-term strategy and direction, and pulls most of the company’s strings himself,” said Stacy Rasgon, a Bernstein analyst.
And many of the company’s executives are relatives of Huang.
Nvidia and Mr Huang have walked a fine line, balancing the demands of Washington and Beijing.
Nvidia is headquartered in California, with the vast majority of its chips produced by the chipmaker TSMC in Taiwan, along with some production in the US and South Korea.
The US restricted the exports of chips to China in 2022, citing it as an issue of national defense.
It has been a huge point of contention between the world’s two superpowers, with Beijing racing to develop its own semiconductor industry.
Mr Huang, who is one of US President Donald Trump’s closest allies in Silicon Valley, has tried to push the administration to loosen restrictions.
He has argued that American companies should be able to compete globally and that it would prevent China’s chip industry from developing too powerfully.
He has had some success. Earlier this year, Washington gave the green light for Nvidia to sell its second-tier chip (the H200) to Chinese companies, so long as they could take a 25% cut.
There have also been reports about Chinese companies illegally getting access to US chip technology through the backdoor.
One company, for example, is a Singapore cloud computing firm, Megaspeed, which is being investigated by the US over suspicions it’s helping get Nvidia AI chips into China.
The Wall Street Journal reports Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy who had an affair with Mr Huang, was previously Megaspeed’s boss.
It was in this capacity that she allegedly met Mr Huang at an Nvidia event in California in 2024. It’s not known how long the affair lasted nor where Ms Huang is now. She has not responded to journalists’ requests for comment.
Now the affair is part of an FBI investigation, with Mr Trump saying he “was amazed” by the allegations.
“I know the FBI is looking into it … I think that he’ll be in good shape,” he said.
US politicians say Congress is likely to tighten China’s access to US chips as part of the fallout while Nvidia’s board has launched an internal investigation.
Beijing has denied the allegations.
“The so-called Chinese spy narrative is purely a groundless accusation, slander, and a smear,” Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said.
Josh Kennedy-White, chief commercial officer at strategic communications firm IN2, said the scandal exposes the danger of making one company and one individual so indispensable to the global AI economy.
“The Huang affair is a reminder that the most valuable target may not be a government official,” he told ABC News.
“When corporate leaders control technologies of national importance, their personal vulnerabilities can become strategic vulnerabilities.”
Jensen Huang has not tweeted or released anything public since he sent staff a letter on Sunday.
“I owe my family and all of you an apology,” he wrote.
“I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

item.title: US fails to show for UN rights review, again
item.description:
The United States boycotted Tuesday a United Nations review of its human rights record for a second time, in an unprecedented snub of a process that all countries traditionally submit to.
US seats were left empty at the world body’s European headquarters in Geneva for the so-called Universal Periodic Review (UPR), which all 193 UN member states undergo every four to five years.
As the review was set to begin, UN Human Rights Council president Sidharto Reza Suryodipuro, of Indonesia, looked at the empty seats behind the US nameplate and noted that “the delegation of the United States is not present in the room.”
The US absence was not a surprise. President Donald Trump’s administration decided shortly after his return to power in January 2025 to halt cooperation with the rights council, and had already boycotted the UPR process last November.
In response, the council at the time had postponed the US review for a year, in the hope that Washington would return to the fold, but to no avail.
But the US State Department told AFP that the administration considers the council an “irredeemable body” that “makes a mockery of human rights,” suggesting that it would not participate in any of its mechanisms, including the UPR.
Washington’s complete non-compliance with the process is unprecedented.
Before the United States, only Israel had previously boycotted its UPR, in early 2013, although it underwent a delayed review later that year.
Some countries have sought postponements since the UPR process began in 2008, while Nicaragua partially boycotted the process, but only after its latest review had already taken place.

item.title: Nvidia and Huang face class-action lawsuit over affair
item.description:
Tech titan Jensen Huang faced fresh turmoil on Tuesday as shareholders sued him and his firm for allegedly misleading them over his affair with an accused Chinese spy.
US-based Rosen Law Firm said it had filed a class-action lawsuit accusing Huang and AI behemoth Nvidia of failing to disclose information to shareholders about his links to the woman who is accused of funneling information to Beijing.
The New York Times reported last month that Taiwanese-born Huang developed a close relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese executive linked to Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed.
The woman is no relation to the 63-year-old Nvidia CEO.
Shares of the chipmaker tumbled after Nvidia’s board opened an inquiry into reports that its CEO had been “the target of a foreign intelligence effort,” which Beijing denies.
China is in a race for tech dominance against the United States, which restricts the export to China of the most cutting-edge silicon chips.
Nvidia, a global leader in producing chips used to train and run AI models, is one of the world’s most valuable companies.
The lawsuit filed in a California federal court on Monday said Huang and Nvidia misled shareholders about the national security concerns raised by the affair, and that their misleading statements “artificially inflated” Nvidia’s share price.
“As a result of Defendants’ wrongful acts and omissions, and the precipitous decline in the market value of the Company’s securities, Plaintiff and other Class members have suffered significant losses and damages,” the lawsuit alleges.
Huang admitted in a message to Nvidia employees released on Sunday that he had been “unfaithful” to his wife.
“My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” he said.
Huang is a central figure in the artificial intelligence boom and a close informal advisor to US President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly opposed regulating the industry so that China does not gain the upper hand.

item.title: Bulgaria motorway pileup kills 11, dozens injured
item.description:
Eleven people died and dozens were injured on Tuesday in a mass pileup on a motorway in southeastern Bulgaria, whose roads rank as the most dangerous in the EU.
Crashes in thick fog snared dozens of vehicles heading in both directions of the highway linking the capital Sofia to the Black Sea city of Burgas.
An estimated 50 cars and trucks were involved in the accident near the city of Yambol, regional governor Georgi Chalakov told the BTA state news agency, as government officials rushed to the scene.
Images showed overturned and smashed cars and trucks mangled together, as well as burnt-out vehicles.
“The toll at this point is 11 dead and 48 injured,” Prime Minister Rumen Radev told reporters.
Radev was meeting EU chief Ursula von der Leyen, who is on a visit to Bulgaria, but the prime minister cancelled his official events scheduled for later Tuesday.
The injured were transported to hospitals in nearby cities. The government dispatched two aircraft equipped with stretchers and medical teams.
Bulgaria saw 71 road fatalities per million inhabitants in 2025, the highest rate in the European Union, according to European Commission figures.
Victims blame the Balkan nation’s high number of traffic deaths on reckless driving, poorly maintained roads and an inefficient justice system.
Romanian Foreign Minister Dan Neculaescu said one Romanian was among the injured and expressed “deepest condolences” to the victims and their families in a post on X.
European Council chief Antonio Costa also said on X he was “deeply saddened to learn of the tragic traffic accident in Bulgaria this morning.”
A total of 456 people were killed in road traffic accidents in Bulgaria in 2025 -- down five percent from the previous year and 27% lower than in 2019.
The EU in 2019 introduced a target to reduce road deaths and serious injuries by 50% by 2030.
A European Commission report in October said that although the EU remains “one of the world’s safest regions for road travel,” the majority of member states were not yet on track to meet the safety target.
The report said that just five of the EU’s 27 countries -- including Bulgaria -- were on track to meet the target.
However, “despite their progress since 2019, Bulgaria and Romania, alongside Croatia, continue to have the highest fatality rates in the EU when measuring deaths per million inhabitants,” the report said.
In 2023, Bulgaria’s parliament adopted stricter penalties for anyone found to be driving under the influence of drugs.
The cars of accused drivers are now impounded until the trial, even when the suspects have no previous criminal record.
Bulgaria’s busy road traffic due to its position as a gateway to the EU is one of the main factors behind the high accident rate, according to experts.
But Bulgaria’s status as the EU’s poorest member state also plays a role, with around half of the cars registered more than 20 years old.

item.title: Chinese worker dies at Barapukuria coal mine in Dinajpur
item.description:
A Chinese worker has died while working underground at the Barapukuria Coal Mine in Parbatipur upazila of Dinajpur.
The deceased, identified as Xing Xiaojun, 43, was found unconscious beside the seal wall of Phase 1305 at the mine on Tuesday morning. He was rushed to Rangpur Medical College Hospital where doctors declared him dead.
Xing was employed in the mine's ventilation section.
Khan Md Zafar Sadik, general manager of the Mine Operation Department of Barapukuria Coal Mining Company Limited (BCMCL), confirmed the incident.
According to mine sources, Xing went underground around 11pm on Monday with two local colleagues to measure gas levels as part of their routine duties.
At one point, he assigned his colleagues to check gas levels in another area and went alone to the seal wall of Phase 1305 for the same task. He could not be traced afterwards.
Khan Md Zafar Sadik said Xing's colleagues alerted the surface control room at around 7am on Tuesday after he failed to return from underground even after his shift ended.
A mine rescue team later launched a search and found him unconscious beside the seal wall of Phase 1305. He was immediately taken to Rangpur Medical College Hospital, where doctors declared him dead.
Some mine workers suspect that a lack of oxygen underground may have caused his death. However, mine authorities have yet to establish the exact cause.
The body is currently being kept in the mortuary of Rangpur Medical College Hospital. The authorities are in contact with the consortium's office in China and the deceased's family regarding the matter.
The consortium is expected to arrange the funeral in accordance with its own procedures.
Abdul Wadud, officer-in-charge of Parbatipur Model Police Station, said an application was being sent for a post-mortem examination. An unnatural death case will also be filed over the incident.
